subtopics.title: Faraday's and Lenz's laws
subtopics.theory_md:
**First law:** whenever the flux linked with a circuit changes, an EMF is induced in it. **Second law:** the magnitude of the EMF equals the rate of change of flux linkage, $e = N\,d\Phi/dt$.

**Lenz's law:** the direction of the induced EMF (and current) is such that it opposes the change that produced it, so $e = -N\,d\Phi/dt$. The minus sign is conservation of energy.

Units: flux in Wb (1 mWb $= 10^{-3}$ Wb), time in s.
subtopics.basics_md: Flux linkage is the number of turns times the flux through them. Change it, in any way, and a voltage appears across the coil. The voltage pushes a current that fights the change.
key_points: Faraday's first law: changing flux linkage induces an EMF
Second law: $e = N\,d\Phi/dt$ (rate of change of flux linkage)
Lenz's law fixes the direction: opposes the cause, hence the minus sign
Lenz's law is a consequence of conservation of energy

questions.model_answer_md:
**Faraday's first law:** whenever the magnetic flux linked with a circuit changes, an EMF is induced in it.

**Faraday's second law:** the magnitude of the induced EMF equals the rate of change of flux linkages: $e = N\,\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}$.

**Lenz's law:** the direction of the induced EMF is such that the current it drives opposes the change of flux that produced it, so $e = -N\,\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}$.
points: First law: changing flux linked with a circuit induces an EMF
Second law: $e = N\,d\Phi/dt$, rate of change of flux linkage

questions.q: A coil of 500 turns links a flux that changes uniformly from 2 mWb to 0.5 mWb in 0.05 s. Find the average induced EMF.
questions.model_answer_md:
$d\Phi = 0.5 - 2 = -1.5$ mWb $= -1.5\times10^{-3}$ Wb, $dt = 0.05$ s

$|e| = N\dfrac{|d\Phi|}{dt} = 500\times\dfrac{1.5\times10^{-3}}{0.05} = 15$ V

The EMF acts to maintain the falling flux (Lenz's law).

subtopics.title: Dynamically and statically induced EMF, inductance
subtopics.theory_md:
**Dynamically induced EMF:** conductor moves in a stationary field (generator): $e = Blv\sin\theta$, direction by **Fleming's right-hand rule**. $\theta$ is the angle between motion and field; $e = 0$ if the motion is along the field.

**Statically induced EMF:** coil stationary, flux changes with current (transformer).
- *Self-induced:* $e = -L\,di/dt$, $L = N\Phi/I = N^2/S$.
- *Mutually induced:* $e_2 = -M\,di_1/dt$, $M = k\sqrt{L_1L_2}$, $0\le k\le1$.

Energy stored: $\tfrac12LI^2$.
subtopics.basics_md: Two ways to change the flux a coil sees: move the coil through the field, or keep the coil still and let the field strength change. The first is a generator; the second is a transformer.
key_points: Dynamic EMF: $e = Blv\sin\theta$, Fleming's right-hand rule, generator action
Static EMF: flux changes in a stationary coil, self or mutual, transformer action
$L = N\Phi/I$, $e = -L\,di/dt$
$M = k\sqrt{L_1L_2}$

subtopics.title: Magnetic terms: retentivity, residual magnetism, coercive force, hysteresis
subtopics.theory_md:
On the B-H loop of a ferromagnet:
- **Magnetic hysteresis:** lag of $B$ behind $H$ over a magnetising cycle; the loop area is the energy lost per cycle per unit volume.
- **Residual magnetism:** $B_r$, the flux density left when $H$ is reduced to zero.
- **Retentivity:** the ability of a material to retain magnetism after $H$ is removed.
- **Coercive force:** $H_c$, the reverse $H$ (A/m) needed to bring $B$ to zero.

Soft iron and silicon steel: narrow loop, low $B_r$ and $H_c$, used for cores. Hard steel: wide loop, used for permanent magnets.
subtopics.basics_md: Push a nail with a magnet and it stays a little magnetic. To demagnetise it you must push the other way. That memory and the reverse push are what the loop shows.
key_points: Hysteresis: $B$ lags $H$; loop area = energy lost per cycle
Residual magnetism: $B$ left at $H = 0$
Retentivity: ability to retain magnetism
Coercive force: reverse $H$ that makes $B$ zero
Cores need a narrow loop, permanent magnets a wide one

options: reverse magnetising force needed to reduce $B$ to zero
questions.why: Option A is residual magnetism; coercive force is the intercept on the $H$ axis.

questions.q: The best material for a transformer core has
options: narrow loop, low retentivity and low coercive force
questions.why: A narrow loop means little energy lost per cycle.

questions.q: What does the area of the hysteresis loop represent? Name the material used to reduce it in transformer cores.
questions.model_answer_md:
The area of the B-H loop is the **energy lost as heat per cycle per unit volume** of the core (hysteresis loss), $P_h = \eta B_m^{1.6} f V$.

It is reduced by using **silicon steel (CRGO)**, which has a narrow loop.
points: Loop area = energy lost per cycle per unit volume
Residual magnetism: magnetism (flux density $B_r$) that remains in a ferromagnetic material after the magnetising force is reduced to zero
Value of $B$ at $H = 0$ on the B-H loop
Retentivity: ability of a magnetic material to retain magnetism after the magnetising force is removed
Measured by residual flux density $B_r$; high for hard steel, low for soft iron
Coercive force $H_c$: reverse magnetising force needed to reduce the residual flux density to zero
Intercept on the $H$ axis of the loop, unit A/m
Hysteresis: lagging of $B$ behind $H$ in a magnetising cycle
$B$ does not return to zero when $H$ is removed; B-H curve is a closed loop
Loop area = hysteresis loss per cycle per unit volume

subtopics.title: Working principle, ratio and DC supply
subtopics.theory_md:
A transformer is a static device that transfers electrical energy between two circuits at the **same frequency** by **mutual induction**. Alternating $V_1$ on the primary sets up an alternating flux in a common laminated core, inducing $E_1$ and $E_2$ in the two windings.

**Transformation ratio** (take $K = N_2/N_1$): $\dfrac{E_2}{E_1}=\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}=\dfrac{N_2}{N_1}=K=\dfrac{I_1}{I_2}$. Ideal: $V_1I_1=V_2I_2$. Rated in **kVA**, so $I_{FL}=\text{VA}/V$.

On **DC** the flux is constant, $d\Phi/dt=0$, so no EMF is induced. Only the small $R_1$ limits the current, $I_1=V/R_1$: the winding burns.
subtopics.basics_md: A transformer needs a changing flux to pass energy across. Alternating current gives a changing flux. DC gives a steady one, which induces nothing.
key_points: Principle: mutual induction, same frequency on both sides
Rated in kVA because loss depends on current and core loss on voltage, independent of pf
On DC: $d\Phi/dt=0$, no EMF, $I=V/R_1$ very large, winding burns

subtopics.title: EMF equation
subtopics.theory_md:
Let $\Phi=\Phi_m\sin\omega t$. Then $e_1=-N_1\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}=N_1\omega\Phi_m\sin(\omega t-90^\circ)$: the EMF **lags the flux by 90 degrees**, with $E_{max}=2\pi fN_1\Phi_m$.

$$E_1=\dfrac{E_{max}}{\sqrt2}=4.44\,fN_1\Phi_m,\qquad E_2=4.44\,fN_2\Phi_m$$

With $\Phi_m=B_mA_i$ (net core area, m$^2$): $E=4.44fNB_mA_i$. EMF per turn is the same in both windings. Alternative: average EMF per turn $=4f\Phi_m$, times form factor $1.11$.
subtopics.basics_md: Flux rises from zero to its peak in a quarter cycle. That fixes the average rate of change, and the sine wave's form factor 1.11 turns average into RMS.
key_points: $e=-N\,d\Phi/dt$ with $\Phi=\Phi_m\sin\omega t$; EMF lags flux by 90 degrees
$E_{max}=2\pi fN\Phi_m$, RMS $E=4.44fN\Phi_m$

subtopics.title: Construction, core and shell type, classification
subtopics.theory_md:
**Parts:** laminated **CRGO silicon-steel** core (silicon cuts hysteresis loss, laminations cut eddy loss); primary and secondary copper windings (LV next to core, HV outside); insulation; for oil-cooled units tank, oil, **conservator** and **breather** (silica gel dries the air entering as oil breathes), Buchholz relay.

**Core type:** windings surround the core, two limbs, single magnetic circuit, cylindrical coils, suits high voltage, easy to repair. **Shell type:** core surrounds the windings, three limbs, centre limb twice as wide, double magnetic circuit, **sandwich** (interleaved) coils, lower leakage, better short-circuit strength, suits low voltage.

**Sandwich winding** reduces leakage flux and reactance, giving better regulation.

**Classification:** core/shell; step-up/step-down; 1-phase/3-phase; power, distribution, instrument; dry/oil cooled.
subtopics.basics_md: Two ways to wrap copper around iron: wires around iron (core) or iron around wires (shell). Shell gives better magnetic coupling; core is easier to build and insulate.

topics.topic: Transformer phasor diagrams and equivalent circuit

subtopics.title: No-load operation and phasor diagram
subtopics.theory_md:
With the secondary open, the primary draws a small $I_0$ (2 to 5 % of rated). It has two components: **magnetising** $I_\mu=I_0\sin\phi_0$ (in phase with $\Phi$, makes the flux) and **working** $I_w=I_0\cos\phi_0$ (in phase with $V_1$, supplies iron loss). $I_0=\sqrt{I_w^2+I_\mu^2}$, $P_i=V_1I_0\cos\phi_0$, pf about 0.1 to 0.3 lagging.

**Phasor construction:** $\Phi$ horizontal reference; $E_1$, $E_2$ lag it by 90 degrees; $V_1=-E_1$; $I_\mu$ along $\Phi$, $I_w$ along $V_1$, $I_0$ their resultant, lagging $V_1$ by $\phi_0$ and leading $\Phi$ by the hysteretic angle $\alpha=90^\circ-\phi_0$.
subtopics.basics_md: An iron-cored coil on AC behaves like a big inductor. Almost all its current just builds the flux (reactive); a thin slice pays for the iron loss (active).
key_points: $I_0$ has $I_\mu$ (along $\Phi$) and $I_w$ (along $V_1$)
$I_0=\sqrt{I_w^2+I_\mu^2}$, $\cos\phi_0=I_w/I_0$ is low
$E_1,E_2$ lag $\Phi$ by 90 degrees; $V_1=-E_1$
Input power at no load is the iron loss $V_1I_0\cos\phi_0$

subtopics.title: On load: MMF balance and constant flux
subtopics.theory_md:
Load current $I_2$ gives an MMF $N_2I_2$ that opposes the flux (Lenz). The tiny flux dip lowers $E_1$, so the primary draws an extra **load component** $I_2'$ with $N_1I_2'=N_2I_2$, i.e. $I_2'=KI_2$, in antiphase with $I_2$. Net MMF returns to $N_1I_0$, so the **flux stays constant** from no load to full load ($\Phi_m\approx V_1/4.44fN_1$).

$$\bar I_1=\bar I_0+\bar I_2'$$

**Lagging-load phasors:** $V_2$ reference; $I_2$ lags by $\phi_2$; $E_2=V_2+I_2(R_2+jX_2)$; $I_2'$ drawn from $-I_2$ scaled by $K$; add $I_0$ to get $I_1$; $V_1=-E_1+I_1(R_1+jX_1)$.
subtopics.basics_md: The secondary current tries to demagnetise the core. The primary instantly pulls extra current to cancel that effect, so the core never notices the load.
key_points: $I_2'=KI_2$, antiphase to $I_2$, cancels the secondary MMF
$\bar I_1=\bar I_0+\bar I_2'$ (phasor sum)
Flux fixed by $V_1\approx4.44fN_1\Phi_m$, so iron loss is constant
Drops $I_1R_1$, $I_1X_1$ added to $-E_1$ to get $V_1$

subtopics.title: Equivalent circuit and referring
subtopics.theory_md:
The model: a **shunt branch** $R_0\parallel X_0$ (core loss and magnetising) with $R_0=V_1/I_w$, $X_0=V_1/I_\mu$, and series $R_1,X_1$ and the secondary $R_2,X_2$ referred across an ideal transformer. Neglecting the shunt branch's drop gives the **approximate circuit**.

**Referring** (take $K=N_2/N_1$): secondary to primary divide impedance by $K^2$, voltage by $K$, multiply current by $K$:
$R_{01}=R_1+R_2/K^2$, $X_{01}=X_1+X_2/K^2$, $Z_{01}=\sqrt{R_{01}^2+X_{01}^2}$.
Primary to secondary multiply by $K^2$: $R_{02}=R_2+K^2R_1=K^2R_{01}$.

Moving to the HV side makes impedance larger.
subtopics.basics_md: Replace the real transformer by an ideal one plus resistors and reactances for the copper, and one parallel branch for the iron. Then move everything to one side so a single circuit remains.
key_points: Shunt branch $R_0\parallel X_0$ for core; series $R_{01}$, $X_{01}$ for windings
Secondary to primary: $Z/K^2$; primary to secondary: $K^2Z$ (with $K=N_2/N_1$)
Referring to HV side makes impedances larger

subtopics.title: Voltage regulation
subtopics.theory_md:
**Voltage regulation** is the fall in secondary terminal voltage from no load to full load, as a fraction of the no-load voltage, with $V_1$ constant:
$$\%\text{reg}=\dfrac{E_2-V_2}{E_2}\times100\approx\dfrac{I_2(R_{02}\cos\phi\pm X_{02}\sin\phi)}{E_2}\times100$$
**+** for lagging pf, **-** for leading. From the circuit referred to the secondary and its phasor diagram ($V_2$ reference, add $I_2R_{02}$ along $I_2$ and $I_2X_{02}$ at 90 degrees ahead), the approximate drop is $I_2R_{02}\cos\phi+I_2X_{02}\sin\phi$. Use $I$, $R$, $X$, $V$ all on the same side. Regulation can be negative for a leading load.
subtopics.basics_md: When you load a transformer, its terminal voltage sags because the windings have impedance. Regulation says how much, as a percentage. Smaller is better.
key_points: Regulation $=(E_2-V_2)/E_2$
Approx: $I_2(R_{02}\cos\phi\pm X_{02}\sin\phi)/E_2$
Plus for lagging, minus for leading

subtopics.title: Open-circuit test
subtopics.theory_md:
**Open-circuit (no-load) test:** apply **rated voltage at rated frequency to the LV winding** (via a variac) with the **HV winding open**. Meters: voltmeter, ammeter and a low-pf wattmeter on the LV side.

- Wattmeter reads the **iron loss** $P_0=P_i$ (copper loss $I_0^2R_1$ is negligible).
- $\cos\phi_0=\dfrac{P_0}{V_0I_0}$, $I_w=I_0\cos\phi_0$, $I_\mu=I_0\sin\phi_0$, $R_0=V_0/I_w$, $X_0=V_0/I_\mu$.

Why LV: rated LV voltage is safe and easy to supply. Why rated voltage: iron loss depends on $B_m$, i.e. on $V$; a lower voltage reads less loss. **pf is low (0.1 to 0.3)** because $I_0$ is mostly magnetising current.
subtopics.basics_md: With the output open, no load current flows, so the only power the transformer takes is what its core wastes. Measure that power at rated voltage and you have the iron loss.
key_points: Done on LV side at rated V and f, HV open
Wattmeter reads iron loss; gives $R_0$, $X_0$, $I_w$, $I_\mu$

subtopics.title: Short-circuit test
subtopics.theory_md:
**Short-circuit test:** short the **LV winding** and supply the **HV winding** from a variac with a **low voltage (5 to 10 % of rated)**, raised until **rated current** flows in the HV winding.

- Flux is tiny, so iron loss is negligible. The wattmeter reads the **full-load copper loss** $P_{sc}=I_{rated}^2R_{eq}$.
- $Z_{eq}=V_{sc}/I_{sc}$, $R_{eq}=P_{sc}/I_{sc}^2$, $X_{eq}=\sqrt{Z_{eq}^2-R_{eq}^2}$, all on the HV side.

subtopics.title: Iron and copper losses
subtopics.theory_md:
A transformer is static: no friction or windage. Only two losses.

**Iron (core) loss $P_i$**, constant at all loads (flux fixed by $V_1$):
- *Hysteresis:* $P_h=\eta B_m^{1.6}fV$. Depends on $B_m$, $f$, volume and material. Cut by **silicon steel**.
- *Eddy current:* $P_e=K_eB_m^2f^2t^2V$. Depends on $B_m$, $f$, lamination thickness $t$, volume, resistivity. Cut by **thin insulated laminations**.

**Copper loss:** $I_1^2R_1+I_2^2R_2=I_2^2R_{02}$, varies as load squared, $P_{cu}=x^2P_{cu,fl}$. Depends on current and winding resistance (temperature).

Small stray and dielectric losses also exist. OC test gives $P_i$; SC test gives $P_{cu}$.
subtopics.basics_md: Iron loss is the price of keeping the flux alive; it does not care about load. Copper loss is the price of pushing current through wire; it grows with the square of current.
key_points: Iron loss (hysteresis + eddy) is constant; copper loss varies as $x^2$
$P_h=\eta B_m^{1.6}fV$, reduced by silicon steel
$P_e=K_eB_m^2f^2t^2V$, reduced by thin laminations

subtopics.theory_md:
**Efficiency** $\eta=\dfrac{\text{output}}{\text{input}}=\dfrac{\text{output}}{\text{output}+\text{losses}}$.

$$\eta=\dfrac{xS\cos\phi}{xS\cos\phi+P_i+x^2P_{cu,fl}}$$
Output is $xS\cos\phi$, **not** $xS$. Iron loss is the same at all loads; copper loss scales as $x^2$. Full-load $P_{cu}=I^2R$ (e.g. $250^2\times0.006=375$ W). Keep W and kW consistent.

If two efficiencies at known loads are given, write the loss $=\text{output}(1/\eta-1)$ for each and solve the two equations in $P_i$ and $P_{cu,fl}$.
subtopics.basics_md: Efficiency is just output divided by output plus whatever is lost. Only the copper loss changes with load; the iron loss stays put.

subtopics.title: Condition for maximum efficiency
subtopics.theory_md:
$\eta=1-\dfrac{P_i}{V_1I_1\cos\phi_1}-\dfrac{I_1R_{01}}{V_1\cos\phi_1}$. For fixed $V_1$ and pf, $\dfrac{d\eta}{dI_1}=\dfrac{P_i}{V_1I_1^2\cos\phi_1}-\dfrac{R_{01}}{V_1\cos\phi_1}=0$, so
$$I_1^2R_{01}=P_i$$
**Efficiency is maximum when variable copper loss equals constant iron loss.**

subtopics.title: All-day efficiency
subtopics.theory_md:
A distribution transformer is energised 24 h but loaded for part of the day. Its performance is judged by **all-day (energy) efficiency**:
$$\eta_{all\ day}=\dfrac{\text{output energy in 24 h (kWh)}}{\text{input energy in 24 h (kWh)}}$$
Iron loss acts for the **full 24 h**: $24P_i$. Copper loss acts only while loaded: $\sum x_k^2P_{cu,fl}t_k$.

So distribution transformers are designed with **low iron loss** (maximum efficiency at a light load), while power transformers, loaded most of the time, can be designed for efficiency near full load.
subtopics.basics_md: Ordinary efficiency is a snapshot; all-day efficiency is energy out over energy in across a daily load cycle. Iron loss is paid every hour, copper loss only when you load it.
key_points: All-day efficiency = output kWh / input kWh in 24 h
Iron loss counted for 24 h; copper loss only for loaded hours

questions.q: Why are a commutator and brushes necessary in a DC machine?
questions.model_answer_md:
- The EMF (and current) in each armature coil is **alternating**, because a coil side passes under N and S poles in turn.
- **Generator:** the commutator reverses the coil connections to the brushes at the instant the coil EMF reverses, so the external output is **unidirectional DC** (mechanical rectifier).
- **Motor:** it reverses the current in a coil as it passes from one pole to the next, so torque stays in **one direction** and rotation is continuous.
- **Brushes** give the sliding contact between the rotating armature and the stationary circuit.

subtopics.title: Generator action and EMF equation
subtopics.theory_md:
**Generator:** the armature is driven; conductors cut flux, EMF is induced (Faraday, direction by **right-hand rule**).

Each conductor cuts $P\Phi$ per revolution, in $60/N$ s: EMF per conductor $=P\Phi N/60$. With $Z/A$ conductors in series per path:
$$E_g=\dfrac{P\Phi ZN}{60A}$$
$N$ in rpm, $\Phi$ in Wb. **Lap:** $A=P$. **Wave:** $A=2$. $Z=$ slots $\times$ conductors per slot.

Terminal voltage: $V=E_g-I_aR_a-V_{brush}$ (total brush drop, two brushes). Generator armature current $I_a=I_L+I_{sh}$ for a shunt generator.

subtopics.title: Motor action, back EMF and speed
subtopics.theory_md:
**Motor principle:** a current-carrying conductor in a field feels a force $F=BIl$ (Fleming's **left-hand rule**); the commutator keeps the torque one way.

**Back EMF:** rotating conductors also generate an EMF that opposes the supply (Lenz). $E_b=\dfrac{P\Phi ZN}{60A}=V-I_aR_a-V_{brush}$. It limits the armature current; a heavier load slows the motor, $E_b$ falls and $I_a$ rises. At start $E_b=0$, so a starter is needed.

**Speed:** $N=\dfrac{60A}{PZ}\cdot\dfrac{E_b}{\Phi}$, i.e. $N\propto E_b/\Phi$, so $\dfrac{N_2}{N_1}=\dfrac{E_{b2}}{E_{b1}}\cdot\dfrac{\Phi_1}{\Phi_2}$.

Shunt motor: $I_a=I_L-I_{sh}$, $I_{sh}=V/R_{sh}$. Torque $T=9.55E_bI_a/N$ N m.
subtopics.basics_md: A spinning armature in a field is a generator even when it is running as a motor. That unwanted voltage opposes the supply, and it settles the speed at which the motor draws just enough current for its load.

$E_b=V-I_aR_a$ (motor) opposes the supply; $E_g=V+I_aR_a$ (generator)
$N\propto E_b/\Phi$
Shunt motor: $I_a=I_L-I_{sh}$, shunt flux constant so $N\propto E_b$

subtopics.title: Types of DC machines and self-excitation
subtopics.theory_md:
**Classified by field excitation.**
- **Separately excited:** field from an independent source.
- **Self-excited** (field from own armature): **shunt** (many thin turns, high $R_{sh}$, in parallel), **series** (few thick turns, in series, $I_L=I_a=I_{se}$), **compound** (both; **long shunt** shunt-field across armature + series field, **short shunt** across armature only; cumulative or differential).

Motor currents: shunt $I_a=I_L-I_{sh}$; series $E_b=V-I_a(R_a+R_{se})$.

**Self-excitation (generator):** residual magnetism gives a small EMF, which drives field current that, if it aids the residual flux, raises the EMF until it builds up. Needs residual magnetism, correct field polarity and field resistance below the critical value.
subtopics.basics_md: The only difference between the types is how the field coil gets its current: from outside, from the armature in parallel, or from the armature in series.

subtopics.title: Speed control and characteristics
subtopics.theory_md:
From $N\propto\dfrac{V-I_aR_a}{\Phi}$, speed is changed by $\Phi$, $R_a$ or $V$.

- **Field (flux) control:** rheostat in series with shunt field; more resistance, weaker $\Phi$, speed **above** rated. Efficient, smooth.
- **Armature resistance control:** resistance in series with armature; speed **below** rated, wasteful ($I_a^2R$), poor regulation.
- **Armature voltage control (Ward-Leonard):** variable $V$, smooth both ways, costly.

**Shunt motor:** $\Phi$ constant, so $T\propto I_a$ (straight line) and $N$ falls only 5 to 15 % with load: **constant-speed motor**. **Series motor:** $T\propto I_a^2$ (then $\propto I_a$), $N\propto1/I_a$ (hyperbola); never start on no load.
subtopics.basics_md: Speed depends on the back EMF over flux. Weaken the flux and it speeds up; add series resistance and it slows down. A shunt motor hardly changes because its flux and drop are tiny.
key_points: Three methods: flux, armature resistance, armature voltage
